cards.explanation: The answer is that Isaac prays to the LORD for her. Isaac prays on behalf of his wife, because she is barren. Then comes the best part: “And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived.” Isaac takes the problem straight to the top, friends. No group chat, no committee.

The answer is True. Rebekah asks, “Why is this happening to me?” and then the text says, “So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD…” Big question, so she takes it straight to Him, friends. That's a good place to bring one.

The answer is two nations. The LORD says, “Two nations are in your womb…” That's a lot of future packed into one small space, bakers. Rebekah came with a question about a struggle and got an answer about whole peoples.
The answer is younger. The LORD says, “…and the older will serve the younger.” That's backwards from how people usually expect things to go, friends. And these twins aren't even born yet.

The answer is Jacob. His brother comes out grasping Esau's heel, so he is named Jacob. He is born in second place and already holding on to the first, bakers. Remember that move, because this boy is just getting started.

The answer is a skillful hunter. Esau becomes “…a skillful hunter, a man of the field…” Skillful, the text says, friends. I get lost between my oven and my cooling rack, so a man who can track down game out in the field impresses me.
The answer is True. Jacob is “…a quiet man who stayed at home.” Esau is the hunter, a man of the field, and Jacob is the one staying home. Two twins, two different ways of spending a day, bakers.
The answer is Esau. Isaac has a taste for wild game, so he loves Esau, the skillful hunter. Meanwhile Rebekah loves Jacob. I think you can already see where this family is headed, friends.

The answer is Edom. Esau asks for some of that red stew, and the text adds, “That is why he was also called Edom.” A second name that comes out of one scene, bakers. I know about names that stick, since mine got carved right into my handle.
The answer is Esau's birthright. Jacob says, “First sell me your birthright…” Esau just wants some stew, and Jacob puts a price on it, friends. That's a big ask for a bowl of dinner.

The answer is that he's about to die, so what good is it. “Look,” says Esau, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” He says it while he's famished, bakers. And I think a hungry man makes some questionable deals.
The answer is False. Jacob doesn't leave it at Esau's word, friends. He says, “Swear to me first…” and Esau swears to Jacob. Then the birthright is sold.

The answer is that he thinks little of it. Esau eats and drinks, gets up and goes away. Then comes the verdict: “Thus Esau despised his birthright.” The verse moves from the meal straight to that word, bakers, and it tells you how he saw it.
